**Short answer:** A mortgage is defined as "the transfer of an interest in specific immoveable property for the purpose of securing the payment of money advanced or to be advanced by way of loan, an existing or future debt, or the performance of an engagement which may give rise to a pecuniary liability" [S1].

**What the sources say:**
*   A mortgage is defined as "the transfer of an interest in specific immoveable property for the purpose of securing the payment of money advanced or to be advanced by way of loan, an existing or future debt, or the performance of an engagement which may give rise to a pecuniary liability" [S1].
*   The person who transfers the property is called a mortgagor, the person who receives the transfer is called a mortgagee, the principal money and interest secured is called the mortgage-money, and the document effecting the transfer is called a mortgage-deed [S1].
*   A simple mortgage occurs when the mortgagor binds themselves personally to pay the mortgage-money without delivering possession of the mortgaged property, and agrees that the mortgagee can cause the property to be sold if payment fails, with the proceeds applied to the mortgage-money [S1].
*   A mortgage by conditional sale occurs when the mortgagor ostensibly sells the property under conditions related to default or payment, unless the condition is in the document effecting the sale [S1].
*   An usufructuary mortgage occurs when the mortgagor delivers possession of the property to the mortgagee, who is authorized to retain possession and receive rents and profits to be used for interest or payment of the mortgage-money [S2].
*   An English mortgage occurs when the mortgagor binds themselves to repay the mortgage-money on a certain date, transfers the property absolutely to the mortgagee, but subject to a proviso that the property will be re-transferred upon payment [S2].
*   A mortgage by deposit of title-deeds involves delivering title documents to a creditor or agent in specified towns with the intent to create security [S2].
*   A mortgage that does not fit the definitions of simple mortgage, mortgage by conditional sale, usufructuary mortgage, English mortgage, or mortgage by deposit of title-deeds is called an anomalous mortgage [S2].
*   If immoveable property is made security for the payment of money to another by act of parties or operation of law, and the transaction is not a mortgage, the latter person has a charge on the property [S3].

**Short answer:** Generally, when a contract is broken, the party who suffers the loss can receive compensation from the party that broke the contract for any loss or damage that naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or which the parties knew when making the contract to be likely to result from the breach [S1][S7]. Compensation is not available for any remote and indirect loss or damage resulting from the breach [S1][S7].

**What the sources say:**
* When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive compensation from the party who has broken the contract for any loss or damage that "naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it" [S1][S7].
* Compensation is not to be given for any "remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach" [S1][S7].
* For failure to discharge an obligation resembling those created by contract, any injured person is entitled to receive the same compensation from the defaulting party as if they had contracted to discharge it and had broken that contract [S1][S7].
* In estimating the loss or damage from a breach, "the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account" [S1][S7].
* If a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of a breach, or if there is any other stipulation by way of penalty, the complaining party is entitled to receive "reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for," regardless of whether actual damage or loss is proven [S4].
* In a suit for specific performance of a contract, the plaintiff may claim compensation for its breach in addition to the specific performance [S3].
* If a court decides that specific performance should not be granted, but that the contract was broken and the plaintiff is entitled to compensation, the court shall award compensation accordingly [S3].
* If a court decides that specific performance should be granted, but it is insufficient to satisfy justice, and compensation for breach should also be made, the court shall award compensation accordingly [S3].
* The court determining compensation under the Specific Relief Act, 1963, shall be guided by the principles in section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [S3].
* The court must adjudge "reasonable compensation to which the plaintiff is entitled from the defendant on breach of the contract," considering the conditions existing on the date of the breach [S8].

**How it may apply:**
* If the contract is broken due to non-performance of a promise, the party suffering the breach has the option of substituted performance through a third party or by their own agency, and can recover the expenses and other costs actually incurred, spent, or suffered from the breaching party [S5].
* If the party suffering the breach gets the contract performed through a third party or by their own agency after giving notice, they cannot claim relief of specific performance against the breaching party [S5].
* A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any damage sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract [S6].

**Uncertain or not covered:** The sources do not specify the exact facts that determine the amount of compensation, other than mentioning that the court must consider the means of remedying the inconvenience [S1][S7] and the conditions existing on the date of the breach [S8]. The sources do not cover compensation claims if the breach involves a contract with a government, other than mentioning that a person entering into a contract with the Government does not necessarily undertake a public duty [S4].

**Short answer:** An agreement made without consideration is generally void, unless it meets specific criteria such as being in writing and registered due to natural love and affection, being a promise to compensate for voluntary action, or being a promise to pay a time-barred debt [S1][S6][S8].

**What the sources say:**
* An agreement made without consideration is void, unless it is in writing and registered, or is a promise to compensate for something done, or is a promise to pay a debt barred by limitation law [S1][S6][S8].
* An agreement made without consideration is void, unless:
    * It is expressed in writing and registered under the law for the time being in force for the registration of documents, and is made on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in a near relation to each other [S1][S6][S8].
    * It is a promise to compensate, wholly or in part, a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor, or something which the promisor was legally compellable to do [S1][S6][S8].
    * It is a promise, made in writing and signed by the person to be charged therewith, or by his agent generally or specially authorized in that behalf, to pay wholly or in part a debt of which the creditor might have enforced payment but for the law for the limitation of suits [S1][S6][S8].
* In any of the cases listed above, such an agreement is a contract [S1][S6][S8].
* Nothing in the Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 25 shall affect the validity, as between the donor and donee, of any gift actually made [S1][S6].

**How it may apply:**
* If an agreement is made on account of natural love and affection between parties in a near relation, it must be expressed in writing and registered under the law for the time being in force for the registration of documents for it to be valid [S1][S6][S8].
* If the agreement is a promise to compensate, it must be a promise to compensate, wholly or in part, a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor, or something which the promisor was legally compellable to do [S1][S6][S8].
* If the agreement is a promise to pay a debt barred by limitation law, it must be a promise, made in writing and signed by the person to be charged therewith, or by his agent generally or specially authorized in that behalf, to pay wholly or in part a debt of which the creditor might have enforced payment but for the law for the limitation of suits [S1][S6][S8].

**Uncertain or not covered:** The sources do not specify what facts are necessary to determine if a specific agreement falls under the exceptions listed in Section 25 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, beyond the general requirements of writing, registration, natural love and affection, compensation, or time-barred debt.

**Short answer:** A court may enforce specific performance of a contract subject to several provisions, including the existence of a valid and enforceable contract [S7]. Specific performance cannot be enforced if certain conditions are met, such as if the contract involves a continuous duty the court cannot supervise [S1] or if the person seeking enforcement has certain bars to relief [S3].

**What the sources say:**
* The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16 [S5].
* Specific performance of a contract cannot be enforced in favour of a person who has obtained substituted performance of contract under section 20 [S3].
* Specific performance cannot be enforced if the contract involves the performance of a continuous duty which the court cannot supervise [S1].
* Specific performance cannot be enforced if the contract is so dependent on the personal qualifications of the parties that the court cannot enforce specific performance of its material terms [S1].
* Specific performance cannot be enforced if the contract is in its nature determinable [S1].
* Specific performance cannot be enforced if the person seeking it "fails to aver and prove that he has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract which are to be performed by him, other than terms the performance of which has been prevented or waived by the defendant" [S3][S8].
* The specific performance of any contract may, in the discretion of the court, be enforced when "there exists no standard for ascertaining actual damage caused by the non-performance of the act agreed to be done" [S8].
* Specific performance may be enforced when "the act agreed to be done is such that compensation in money for its non-performance would not afford adequate relief" [S8].
* The jurisdiction to order specific performance of a contract is based on the existence of a valid and enforceable contract [S7].

**How it may apply:**
* Specific performance may be enforced when the act agreed to be done is in the performance wholly or partly of a trust, except as otherwise provided in the Specific Relief Act, 1963 [S4].
* The court may enforce specific performance even if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of its breach, provided the court is satisfied that the sum was named only for securing performance and not as an option to pay money in lieu of specific performance [S2].
* If a contract is for the non-performance of which compensation in money is an adequate relief, it may not be specifically enforceable [S1][S6].
* The court may enforce specific performance in certain cases, such as where the suit is for the execution of a formal deed of partnership, and the parties have commenced to carry on the business of the partnership [S6].

**Uncertain or not covered:** The sources do not specify all the facts that must be present for a court to enforce specific performance, other than the general requirements listed above. Missing facts include the specific nature of the contract, the details of the alleged breach, and whether the contract falls under any exceptions or provisions not detailed in the provided sections.

**Short answer:** Generally, courts have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature unless the cognizance is expressly or impliedly barred [S1][S6]. The courts that can try suits depend on the specific context, such as whether the suit relates to infrastructure projects or if the matter is governed by a special enactment [S2][S3].

**What the sources say:**
* The Courts shall have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature unless their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred [S1][S6].
* A suit in which the right to property or to an office is contested is considered a suit of a civil nature, even if the right depends entirely on the decision of questions about religious rites or ceremonies [S1].
* The State Government may designate certain Civil Courts as Special Courts to try suits under the Specific Relief Act, 1963, concerning contracts related to infrastructure projects [S2].
* Where Revenue Courts are governed by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the State Government may declare that certain provisions of the Code shall not apply to those Courts, or shall only apply with modifications prescribed by the State Government [S3].
* Every suit must be instituted in the Court of the lowest grade competent to try it [S4].
* The Order under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, applies to High Courts, City Civil Courts, and Courts of Small Causes, among others [S5].

**How it may apply:**
* The jurisdiction of civil courts to try suits of a civil nature is described as "very expansive," and any statute that excludes this jurisdiction is considered an exception to the general rule [S7].
* If a statute excludes the jurisdiction of civil courts, the party asserting that exclusion must establish it, as "Ouster of civil court’s jurisdiction is not to be readily inferred" [S7].
* For matters arising under the Tenancy Act, civil courts are expressly barred from trying a suit or proceeding if a remedy is provided by way of a suit, application, appeal, or otherwise under that Act [S6].

**Uncertain or not covered:** The sources do not provide a comprehensive list of all courts that can try civil suits across all circumstances; rather, they describe general rules and specific exceptions for certain types of suits or Acts [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5]. The specific facts determining jurisdiction, such as the nature of the dispute or the governing statute, are necessary to determine which court has jurisdiction.

**Short answer:** Under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, "Res judicata" means that "No Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a Court competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such Court" [S1].

**What the sources say:**
* Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, states that "No Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a Court competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such Court" [S1].
* The doctrine of res judicata is founded on public policy, aiming for an end to the same litigation [S3].
* Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, is described as merely statutory recognition of the principle of res judicata, and the section is not considered exhaustive of the general principle of law [S3].
* The main purpose of the doctrine is that "once a matter has been determined in a former proceeding, it should not be open to parties to reagitate the matter again and again" [S3].
* The Code deals with res judicata in Section 11, and for the bar of res judicata to apply, several essential requirements must be fulfilled, including that the matter must be directly and substantially in issue in both the former and later suit, and the prior suit must be between the same parties or persons claiming under them [S4].
* The doctrine of res judicata is founded on public policy, and an issue of fact or law or mixed question of fact and law, which was in issue in an earlier suit and was adjudicated or allowed uncontested, becomes final and binds the parties [S7].
* The "matter in issue" in Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure means "the right litigated between the parties i.e. the facts on which the right is claimed or denied and the law applicable to the determination of that issue" [S8].

**How it may apply:**
* The matter directly and substantially in issue must have been alleged by one party and either denied or admitted, expressly or impliedly, by the other [S1].
* Any matter that might and ought to have been made a ground of defence or attack in the former suit shall be deemed to have been a matter directly and substantially in issue in that suit [S1].
* The provisions of Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, apply to a proceeding for the execution of a decree, and references to a suit, issue, or former suit in this section are construed as references to the corresponding proceeding for the execution of the decree, question arising in such proceeding, and a former proceeding for the execution of that decree, respectively [S2].
* An issue heard and finally decided by a Court of limited jurisdiction, which was competent to decide that issue, shall operate as res judicata in a subsequent suit, even if that Court was not competent to try the subsequent suit or the suit in which the issue was subsequently raised [S2].
* The doctrine cannot apply to a pure question of law unrelated to facts, nor can it apply to the interpretation of a statute touching the jurisdiction of a court, even if the question was raised between the parties [S7][S8].
* A question relating to jurisdiction of a court or an interpretation of a statute cannot be deemed to have been finally determined by an erroneous decision of a court [S7][S8].

**Uncertain or not covered:** The sources do not specify the exact facts that must be present for a specific case to determine if res judicata applies, other than listing the general requirements under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

**Short answer:** A court may grant a temporary injunction under Order XXXIX Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, if it is proved by affidavit or otherwise that certain conditions are met [S1].

**What the sources say:**
* A temporary injunction may be granted if it is proved by affidavit or otherwise that any property in dispute in a suit is in danger of being wasted, damaged or alienated by any party to the suit, or wrongfully sold in execution of a decree [S1].
* A temporary injunction may be granted if it is proved by affidavit or otherwise that the defendant threatens, or intends, to remove or dispose of his property with a view to "defrauding" his creditors [S1].

**Short answer:** A court may reject a plaint in several circumstances, including if it does not disclose a cause of action, if the claimed relief is undervalued and the plaintiff fails to correct it, if the plaint is insufficiently stamped and the plaintiff fails to supply the required stamp-paper, or if the suit appears to be barred by any law [S1][S4].

**Short answer:** The market value of land can be determined by several criteria, including the market value specified in the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, the average sale price of similar land in the nearest vicinity, or the consented compensation amount agreed upon for private companies or public private partnership projects, whichever is higher [S1]. **Short answer:** If the Sub-Registrar refuses to register a document because someone denies its execution, a person claiming under the document may apply to the Registrar within thirty days to establish their right to have the document registered [S1]. If the refusal is on a ground other than denial of execution, an appeal can be made to the Registrar within thirty days [S3].

**What the sources say:**
* If a Sub-Registrar refuses to register a document because any person by whom it purports to be executed, or their representative or assign, denies its execution, any person claiming under such document, or their representative, assign, or agent, may apply to the Registrar to whom the Sub-Registrar is subordinate within thirty days after the order of refusal [S1].
* The application to the Registrar in the case of denial of execution must be in writing and include a copy of the reasons recorded under Section 71, with the statements verified by the applicant [S1].
* If the Sub-Registrar refuses to register a document on a ground other than denial of execution, an appeal can be presented to the Registrar within thirty days from the date of the order [S3].
* The Sub-Registrar must record reasons for refusing to register a document, unless the property is not situated within their sub-district, and must endorse the refusal on the document [S2].
* If the Registrar refuses to order the document to be registered under Section 72 or Section 76, any person claiming under the document may file a suit in the Civil Court within thirty days after the order of refusal [S5].

**How it may apply:**
* If the refusal is due to denial of execution, the process involves applying to the Registrar within thirty days, which requires a written application, a copy of the reasons from Section 71, and verification of the statements [S1].
* If the refusal is on a ground other than denial of execution, an appeal to the Registrar is possible within thirty days [S3].
* If the Registrar refuses to order registration under Section 72 or Section 76, a civil suit can be filed within thirty days [S5].

**What the sources say:**

**How it may apply:**
